name: Marco Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the die-cutter at a cardboard box plant on the edge of town. Big sheets of corrugated board come off the corrugator, and my machine cuts and creases them into flat boxes for a supermarket chain and a few fruit growers. I set the cutting forms, feed the board, watch for crushed flutes and stack the bundles for the strapping machine. Shifts rotate, two weeks of days and one week of lates.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a tricky job right, like a fruit tray with lots of folds, when it comes out clean first time. What wears me out is the dust and the pay, which is below the big packaging firm in the next valley. I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a hairdresser, and we're saving for a deposit on a flat, but honestly we've got about three weeks' money and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never thought it'd be as big as they said. At work we'd shrug and get on with it. Online I don't say much, maybe a joke in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me, because my job doesn't change. But fine isn't great when you're on lower pay and trying to buy a flat. I'd still be stuck on the same money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and ask about moving up to the corrugator, which pays a bit more. I'd use the AI chat now and then, like I do, to check my payslip or write an email. I'd keep putting a little into the deposit pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not thrilled, not scared. Just a bit flat, like the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're saving for a deposit with three weeks' money. How's that going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. We put in a hundred a month when we can, and some months we can't. At a hundred a month, Ana (his girlfriend) and I will have a flat deposit by about the time we're 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything at the box plant changed lately, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put in a new strapping machine last year and one bloke moved to the warehouse. Nobody lost a job, but you notice. Orders are steady because people always need boxes.

say: I'd say I **never thought** AI would be as big as they said.
I'd make a **joke** in the group chat and get on with it.
think: I think my **job doesn't change**, which is fine.
I think fine isn't great on **lower pay** while saving for a flat.
do: Ask about moving up to the **corrugator**, which pays a bit more.
Use the **AI chat** now and then for payslips and emails.
Keep adding a hundred a month to the **deposit pot**.
feel: **Okay**, a bit flat, neither thrilled nor scared.
S0.quote: At a hundred a month, Ana (his girlfriend) and I will have a flat deposit by about the time we're 40.
fieldNote: Marco's worry is slow **deposit savings** on low pay, not AI.
He has already seen a **strapping machine** move a colleague, which he noticed.
He's pragmatic and uses AI **lightly** for admin.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor about moving to the corrugator
Add a hundred a month to the flat deposit
Use the AI chat to check payslips and write emails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say most of us will be okay if we adapt a bit. At work I'd say watch the office, they'll feel it first. Online I'd say people should learn the basics of the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the robots are the bit that worries me, because stacking bundles off my die-cutter is just the kind of thing a robot arm does. Maybe not in two years, but in five. And with few other factories round here, I'd have nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to go on the course for the new strapping and stacking machines, once one of the lads has tried it. I'd use AI a bit more to learn how the machines work. I'd keep saving, maybe less for the flat and more for a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. Like I can see the cloud but it's not raining yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you see it first at the box plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the office first, with the ordering and the quotes done on a computer. Then a robot on the stacking end, because that's heavy, boring work. If a robot stacks the bundles off my die-cutter, the box plant needs one operator where it now needs two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Ana's work, would it change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I think. A robot isn't going to cut hair any time soon. Ana might be the safe one in our house, which she'd love to tell everyone.

say: I'd say most people will be **okay** if they adapt a bit.
I'd tell people to learn the **basics** of the new tools.
think: I think a **robot arm** stacking bundles could halve the operators.
I think there are **few other factories** nearby to go to.
do: Ask for the course on **stacking machines** once a colleague has tried it.
Use **AI** more to learn how the machines work.
Shift some savings from the flat to a **safety net**.
feel: **Uneasy turning into worried**, like a cloud before rain.
S1.quote: If a robot stacks the bundles off my die-cutter, the box plant needs one operator where it now needs two.
fieldNote: Marco sees the **stacking end** of his own machine as the weak point.
He waits for a **colleague** to try a course first, fitting his steady style.
He notes **Ana's hairdressing** may be the safer income, with some humour.

steps.text: Sign up for the stacking machine course after a colleague tries it
Use AI to learn how the box plant machines work
Move part of the deposit savings into an emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is big and the government needs to get a plan together. At work I'd tell people to start looking now, not wait. Online I'd share anything useful about training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm out by 2031. The office goes in 2028, and then the robots do the die-cutting and stacking. I'm average at the job, I don't have a trade, and I've got three weeks' money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrician's course as soon as it's announced, because wiring robots into old buildings needs people for a while. I'd stop saving for the flat and put it all into living costs. I'd ask my dad if we could stay with him if things got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd be moving, not frozen. Sitting still would be worse than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI in 2028, robots around 2031. What does that three-year gap mean on your machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is time to get one qualification, if I start right away and do it in the evenings. Three years is just enough to get an electrician's ticket, if I study every evening after my shift at the box plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gone, at least for now. We'd keep renting. Ana says she'd rather rent and sleep than buy and worry.

say: I'd say the **government** needs a plan for this.
I'd tell colleagues to **start looking** now, not wait.
think: I think I'm **out by 2031**, once robots do the cutting and stacking.
I think being **average** with three weeks' money leaves me exposed.
do: Start an **electrician's course** in the evenings as soon as it's announced.
Stop saving for the **flat** and cover living costs.
Ask my **dad** if we could stay with him if things got bad.
S2.quote: Three years is just enough to get an electrician's ticket, if I study every evening after my shift at the box plant.
fieldNote: Marco treats the **three-year gap** as exactly one qualification's worth of time.
He'd drop the **flat plan**, which matters a lot to him.
He expects to **lose the job** but still acts, so alarmed rather than panicked.

steps.text: Start an evening electrician's course straight away
Pause flat deposit saving to cover living costs
Ask his dad about staying with him if money runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a bit of time, so let's plan properly. At work I'd say don't panic, but don't sit still. Online I'd probably share what courses are good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose the die-cutter job, but later, and I'd have time to get a trade. I'd be 35 with an electrician's ticket, which is better than 32 with nothing. It still worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see how other plants handle it, then start the electrician's course. I'd keep saving for the flat but slower. I'd keep using AI to help me study, because it's good at explaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see a way through. It's like a long job on the die-cutter, you just do it fold by fold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, and robots around 2034, would you do it differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, slower and smarter. With five years, I'd watch what the bigger packaging firm does before I spend money on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Pedro, who's an electrician. He'd tell me straight whether it's worth it.

say: I'd say there's **a bit of time** to plan properly.
I'd tell colleagues **don't panic**, but don't sit still.
think: I think I'd still **lose the die-cutter** job, just later.
I think 35 with an **electrician's ticket** beats 32 with nothing.
do: Wait a year to see how **other plants** handle it.
Start the **electrician's course** after that year.
feel: **Worried**, but I can see a way through.
S3.quote: With five years, I'd watch what the bigger packaging firm does before I spend money on a course.
fieldNote: Marco would **watch others** first, then commit, true to his steady style.
He trusts his **cousin Pedro** over any official adviser.
He keeps the **flat plan** alive here, which signals a bit more control.

steps.text: Watch how the bigger packaging firm handles robots for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, people just need to get organised. At work I'd say get a trade while you've got time. Online I'd probably not say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be all right. I'd get the electrician's ticket over a few years, keep the die-cutter job meanwhile, and maybe buy the flat with Ana.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician's course in a year or two, once we've got the deposit nearly done. I'd keep saving. I'd use AI tools when the plant brings them in, like everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little uneasy. It's far enough off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. What does that do to your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could still buy the flat, then retrain. Ten years means Ana (his girlfriend) and I could buy the flat first and I could retrain second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you stay at the box plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe as the one who fixes the robots, if I'm an electrician by then. That'd be a nice twist.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if people get organised.
I'd tell colleagues to **get a trade** while there's time.
think: I think I'd be **all right** with time to retrain.
I think we could still **buy the flat** with Ana.
do: Start the **electrician's course** in a year or two.
Use **AI tools** when the plant brings them in.
S4.quote: Ten years means Ana (his girlfriend) and I could buy the flat first and I could retrain second.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Marco keep the **flat** and retrain in order.
He imagines staying as the **robot fixer**, a hopeful twist.
His mood is **uneasy** because his own income looks safe for years.

steps.text: Start an electrician's course within two years
Keep saving for the flat deposit with Ana

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to drop the flat and cram a whole trade into three years. What would help is evening courses that are free and a bit of money while you study, so you don't have to choose between rent and learning. I'm not scared of learning a trade, I'm scared of learning it while the rent's due.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about small towns. In the city there are ten factories, and here there's three. That's the bit that changes everything.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of learning a trade, I'm scared of learning it while the rent's due.
portrait: Marco, 27, runs a **die-cutter** at a cardboard box plant and saves slowly for a flat with his girlfriend Ana.
He is **pragmatic**, uses AI for small tasks and waits to see others try new things first.
His plan in the faster pictures is an **electrician's ticket**, studied in the evenings.
He goes from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, and back to uneasy with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd drop the flat plan and cram a trade into three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Free evening courses** and some money while studying, so rent doesn't clash with learning.
